main_damage_causes: Loss of the classroom quiz scene (excluded per non-theatrical instruction) removes the foundational demonstration of Lockhart's narcissistic pedagogy, thinning the sustained portrait of his incompetence as a teacher from a pattern into isolated incidents

Absence of multiple mid-film character scenes (Greenhouse Three monologue, re-enactment lessons, Valentine's Day, Colin Creevey corridor) means the film Lockhart is only visible at plot-functional moments rather than as a persistent, grinding presence in Harry's daily school life — reducing him from a character to a series of set pieces

The film loses several scenes showing Lockhart's hypocrisy and self-delusion in private or semi-private registers (lecturing Harry on fame-seeking while being more fame-hungry himself, patronising Hagrid, claiming credit for stopping the attacks) so the film version reads as straightforwardly vain rather than as the specific variety of deluded fraud Rowling constructs

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart's first DADA class (quiz scene cut per non-theatrical exclusion)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Lockhart's quiz as a defining moment of his narcissism and incompetence as a teacher: questions solely about his favourite colour (lilac), birthday gifts, and secret ambitions. The class reacts with disbelief and silent laughter. This scene crystallises his self-obsession and sets up the pixie disaster as part of a coherent portrait of a fraud performing competence.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The quiz scene is excluded from the theatrical release per the non-theatrical exclusion instruction. The film's first class jumps directly to Lockhart's introduction speech and then the pixie release, losing the sustained comedic portrait of his narcissistic pedagogy and the class's dawning realisation of his absurdity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The quiz is the clearest single demonstration that Lockhart treats his teaching post purely as a vehicle for self-promotion. Without it, the film loses a full beat of character-building that establishes the pattern of incompetence before the pixie disaster. The film Lockhart still reads as vain, but the texture of his fraudulence as educator is thinner.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart's classroom, pixie lesson (Film Scene 3/42)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after the pixies are released and chaos ensues, Lockhart attempts his spell ('Peskipiksi Pesternomi'), it fails completely, a pixie steals his wand, and he dives under his desk to avoid being hit by the falling chandelier. He then instructs Harry, Ron, and Hermione to put the pixies back and sweeps out, leaving them to deal with the mess.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the broad outline but Lockhart joins the stampede to the door rather than diving under his desk — he flees with the students rather than cowering separately beneath his own furniture. The specific humiliation of hiding under his desk (while Neville falls from the chandelier) is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor loss. The desk-hiding is a precise comic beat that underlines his cowardice in a more pathetic, specific way than simply fleeing. The film version still conveys cowardice but loses the particular quality of his shameless self-preservation while a student dangles from the ceiling.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Greenhouse Three / Whomping Willow encounter (Film: absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lockhart intercept Harry outside Greenhouse Three, dismiss Professor Sprout by closing the door in her face, and deliver a lengthy monologue blaming Harry's flying-car stunt on the 'taste for publicity' Lockhart himself gave him. He compares Harry's scar unfavourably to his own Witch Weekly Most-Charming-Smile Award, tells Harry he was 'just as much of a nobody' at twelve, and gives a hearty wink before striding off. This scene is key to establishing Lockhart's delusional self-importance and his specific dynamic with Harry: he genuinely believes Harry craves fame like he does.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus at all. The film has no equivalent moment where Lockhart privately lectures Harry about fame and publicly patronises him outside a class.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The greenhouse scene is one of the richest character moments for Lockhart in the book: it shows him as not merely vain but genuinely convinced of his own worldview, incapable of reading Harry's contempt, and condescending in a specific, absurd way. Its absence means the film Lockhart lacks this private register of delusion — we only see him perform for crowds, never embarrass himself one-on-one in a sustained way before the climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Colin Creevey corridor / signed photo scene (Film: absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lockhart clamp Harry to his side when he finds him with Colin Creevey, stage a double portrait, tell the crowd to move along, and then lecture Harry that handing out signed photos 'looks a tad bigheaded' — while himself keeping a stack handy at all times. He escorts Harry to his classroom with his arm around him, burning with humiliation. This scene shows Lockhart's hypocrisy (lecturing Harry on self-promotion while doing exactly that) and his social obliviousness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus. The film's Harry-Colin dynamic exists but Lockhart does not insert himself into it in this way.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene provides the clearest illustration of Lockhart's hypocrisy — warning Harry against the very behaviour he exemplifies — and his physical imposition on Harry (clamping him to his side). The film loses this specific comedic register of oblivious double-standard, making Lockhart's vanity slightly less layered.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart's DADA lessons: dramatic re-enactments (Film: absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes a sustained pattern across multiple lessons: Lockhart reads from his books and re-enacts dramatic moments, casting Harry as a Transylvanian villager, a yeti with a head cold, a vampire on a lettuce diet, and a werewolf. This establishes a recurring dynamic of Harry being humiliated, Lockhart being obliviously self-aggrandising, and the class enduring a useless teacher.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has no scenes showing these re-enactment lessons. After the pixie disaster, the film does not depict Lockhart's subsequent classroom behaviour at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The re-enactment lessons are important to sustaining the portrait of Lockhart as an ongoing, grinding failure as a teacher — not just a one-off with the pixies. They also build Harry's specific resentment and the class's collective suffering. Without them, Lockhart's classroom incompetence reads as a single incident rather than a consistent pattern.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart claims credit for stopping the attacks (Film: absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lockhart overheard by Harry telling McGonagall he's personally responsible for the cessation of attacks, tapping his nose and winking, claiming the culprit must have known Lockhart was close to catching him. This is a key beat of his delusional self-importance intersecting with the actual plot.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus. The film does not show Lockhart making this claim.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor loss. The scene adds a specific layer of Lockhart's fraudulence — not just taking credit for others' past deeds but actively claiming credit for plot-relevant events happening in real time. Its absence slightly reduces his role as a comic obstacle to the mystery's resolution.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Valentine's Day decoration (Film: absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lockhart organise a Valentine's Day event with dwarf cupids delivering singing valentines, announcing it cheerfully at breakfast in lurid pink robes, citing the forty-six cards he himself received, and suggesting colleagues show Lockhart-approved 'spirit.' McGonagall's jaw muscles work, Snape looks as though fed Skele-Gro. This scene demonstrates Lockhart's social power (he can impose school-wide events) and his total unawareness of colleagues' contempt.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No Valentine's Day scene appears in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Valentine's scene is the clearest demonstration that Lockhart has genuine institutional influence — Dumbledore permits his schemes — and the most vivid picture of staff suffering under him. Its absence removes a dimension of his character: that his delusion extends to believing he is beloved by colleagues who visibly despise him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart visits Hagrid / advice on kelpies (Film: absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Harry, Ron, and Hermione hide behind a bush to watch Lockhart leave Hagrid's hut, loudly offering to lend Hagrid his book on kelpie removal, implying his superiority. Hagrid later describes Lockhart as having given unsolicited advice. Hagrid tells Harry he told Lockhart Harry is more famous without trying, and Lockhart didn't like it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss. The scene develops Lockhart's relationship with Hagrid (condescension toward a colleague he considers beneath him) and gives Hagrid a small moment of defending Harry against Lockhart's jealousy. It adds texture to Lockhart's snobbery but its absence is not structurally significant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart's fan mail detention, voice heard in wall (Film Scene 49)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes the detention as a long, grinding ordeal: Harry addresses envelopes for hours while Lockhart prattles about fame ('Fame's a fickle friend'), and Harry hears the mysterious voice in the wall. Lockhart is oblivious and dismissive, suggesting Harry is drowsy. The scene ends with Lockhart remarking Harry mustn't expect 'a treat like this' every detention — the last word of self-satisfied obliviousness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the core of this scene faithfully — candlelit office, fan mail, Lockhart's self-congratulation, Harry hearing the voice, Lockhart not hearing it, and Lockhart's dismissive response. The film version is slightly compressed but the characterisation is consistent with the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Largely faithful. Minor compression means the full texture of the four-hour ordeal and Lockhart's final parting line about not expecting this 'treat' every time are lost, slightly softening the relentlessness of his self-absorption, but the core damage is minimal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart after Mrs Norris Petrified, in his office (Film Scene 59)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when the group convenes in Lockhart's office, the photographs on his walls show Lockharts dodging out of sight with their hair in rollers — a comic detail of vanity. Lockhart hovers around Dumbledore making suggestions, claims he knows the countercurse, references Ouagadougou, counts murders he's prevented until Dumbledore cuts him off, and then tries to claim credit when Dumbledore announces Mrs Norris is Petrified ('Ah! I thought so!'). Snape coldly corrects him on the Mandrake Restorative Draught.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains Lockhart's Ouagadougou reference, his countercurse claim, and his 'Precisely! So unlucky I wasn't there' response to Dumbledore. The hair-in-rollers detail is absent. The specific exchange about the Mandrake Restorative Draught and Snape's correction ('I believe I am the Potions master at this school') is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Snape correction scene is a small but pointed moment showing Lockhart overreaching into Snape's domain and being publicly humiliated by a peer — it reinforces his lack of actual competence. Its absence is a minor loss. The hair-in-rollers detail is a nice vanity joke but inconsequential.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Dueling Club, Lockhart's blocking demonstration (Film Scene 70)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lockhart attempt a 'complicated sort of wiggling action' with his wand to demonstrate a blocking charm and drop it, then cover with 'Whoops — my wand is a little overexcited.' When Harry asks to see the blocking charm again, Lockhart tells him to 'just do what I did' without having demonstrated anything useful. This is a precise beat of incompetence-concealed-by-bluster.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus includes the Dueling Club scene but does not appear to include the specific wand-drop/blocking demonstration moment. The film moves from Snape disarming Lockhart to Snape suggesting Harry and Malfoy duel, with Lockhart selecting them himself ('Let's have a volunteer pair. Potter, Weasley, how about you?'). The blocking demonstration with the dropped wand is not evidenced in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss. The dropped-wand moment is a tight comic beat that shows Lockhart's technical incompetence in his own supposed area of expertise. Without it, his failure at the Dueling Club reads as a single embarrassment (being disarmed by Snape) rather than compounded by an inability even to demonstrate a basic blocking charm.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart allows Harry and Ron to ditch his escort to History of Magic (Film: absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Harry and Ron deliberately flatter Lockhart into abandoning his escort duty by agreeing with his complaints about security measures being unnecessary, allowing them to slip away to Moaning Myrtle's bathroom. Lockhart is so easily manipulated by agreement that he abandons a duty McGonagall assigned specifically because Harry tells him he agrees.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss. The scene shows Lockhart as specifically susceptible to flattery to the point of professional negligence — a precise character note. Its absence removes one demonstration of how his vanity makes him functionally useless as a protector, though this is established by other means.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart removes Harry's bones after Quidditch match (Film Scene 65)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Harry explicitly say 'No!' and 'I'll keep it like this, thanks' and 'Why can't I just go to the hospital wing?' Lockhart overrides him, performs the spell, and removes all bones. His response is the classic Lockhart non-apology: 'Ah... the point is, the bones are no longer broken.' Ron's reaction ('if Harry had wanted deboning he would have asked') captures the absurdity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains this scene faithfully. Harry protests ('No... no... not you'), Lockhart overrides him ('Poor boy doesn't know what he's saying'), performs the spell, and delivers the same non-apology. Hagrid's reaction ('He doesn't 'ave any bones at all!') replaces Ron's line. The characterisation is consistent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Essentially faithful. The film shifts the reactive punchline from Ron to Hagrid, which slightly reduces the peer-group mockery of Lockhart, but the core portrait of his disastrous overconfidence is intact.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart's staffroom entrance / teachers cornering him (Film Scene 125)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes Lockhart entering the staffroom beaming, having 'dozed off,' unaware of the gravity of the situation, and then being cornered by colleagues who cite his own boasts back at him — Sprout, Flitwick, and Snape each with specific quotes. Lockhart blanches and physically transforms: 'He didn't look remotely handsome anymore. His lip was trembling, and in the absence of his usually toothy grin, he looked weak-chinned and feeble.' This is the moment the mask fully slips.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains this scene with good fidelity: Lockhart enters cheerily ('So sorry. Dozed off. What have I missed?'), Snape and McGonagall cite his boasts, he stammers ('D-did I? I don't recall...') and caves ('V-very well. I'll — I'll be in my office, getting — getting ready.'). The physical description of his collapse is conveyed through Kenneth Branagh's performance per the stage directions, and the stammering dialogue matches the book's intent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Largely faithful. The specific line about looking 'weak-chinned and feeble' is a prose observation that cannot be directly filmed, but the scene's function — the unmasking of the fraud — is intact. Minor execution difference only.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart's office, attempted flight and Memory Charm confession (Film Scene 128)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lockhart explicitly confess the full mechanics of his fraud: he tracked down the real heroes, asked how they did it, then Obliviated them. He also explicitly mentions the Armenian warlock and the witch with a harelip who banished the Bandon Banshee. He then attempts a Memory Charm on Harry and Ron before being disarmed. The confession is detailed, self-justifying, and reveals genuine cynicism ('My books wouldn't have sold half as well if people didn't think I'd done all those things').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the Armenian warlock reference, the core confession ('My books wouldn't have sold half as well...'), the Memory Charm attempt, and Harry's Expelliarmus. The film adds a line not in the book corpus: 'You want fame, you have to be prepared for a long, hard slog' — framing Lockhart as oddly self-aware about the labour of fraud. Ron's line 'Is there anything you can do?' and Lockhart's pivot to revealing his Memory Charm skill is handled differently: in the film it flows more naturally as a threat. The harelip detail is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Mostly faithful. The added 'long, hard slog' line gives film Lockhart a faint trace of self-awareness about his own cynicism that the book Lockhart lacks — book Lockhart is more purely delusional. This is a small but real tonal shift. The harelip detail is a minor loss. Overall the confession scene functions correctly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Lockhart in the tunnel, faking unconsciousness / seizing Ron's wand (Film Scene 132)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lockhart's knees give way at the sight of the snakeskin, then he dives at Ron, knocking him down, seizes his wand, and delivers the 'The adventure ends here, boys!' speech including the threat to bind a limited edition in snakeskin. He then fires the Memory Charm with Ron's defective wand, which backfires.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Lockhart pass out entirely ('THUD! They turn. Lockhart has passed out. Heart of a lion, this one.'), then Ron kneels by him and Lockhart's eyes open and he 'quick as a fox' snatches Ron's wand. The 'adventure ends here' speech is retained with added detail about binding a limited edition in snakeskin. This is consistent with the book in substance though the staging (full faint vs. knees giving way) differs slightly.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor staging difference. The film's full faint followed by quick recovery is slightly more comedic and less pathetic than the book's collapsing knees. Both convey his cowardice and opportunism. The core beat is intact.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - St Mungo's Hospital visit (Books 4/5 reference — absent from film series covered by corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book (Order of the Phoenix) shows Lockhart in the permanent spell damage ward at St Mungo's, cheerfully oblivious, offering autographs, having signed photos to himself on his wall, receiving fan mail from Gladys Gudgeon, and asking if Harry and the others live there. He has childlike joy and no memory of who he was. This is both comic and faintly tragic.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus provided, which covers only Chamber of Secrets. Its absence is noted but falls outside the scored film.
